parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old Norse alfr, probably through Russian альв (alʹv). Related to Ukrainian ельф (elʹf).
Inherited from Old East Slavic варѧгъ (varęgŭ), from Old Norse væringi.

From older form гаръ (har, “tribute”), which derived from Old Norse herra (“lord, king”). Cognate with Belarusian гарны (harny), obsolete Pannonian Rusyn гарни (harni), Polish harny. Equivalent to гаръ (har) + -ний (-nyj). See also Bulgarian харен (haren) and Romanian harnic.
From older form гаръ (har, “tribute”), which derived from Old Norse herra (“lord, king”). Cognate with Polish harno. Equivalent to гаръ (har) + -но (-no). Parsable as гарний (harnyj) + -о (-o).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian крюкъ, крукъ (krjuk, kruk), from Old Norse krókr, from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz.
From Old East Slavic сельдь (selĭdĭ) (1497), from earlier *сьлдь (*sĭldĭ), from Old Norse síld. Compare Belarusian селядзе́ц (sjeljadzjéc), Russian се́льдь (sélʹdʹ).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ꙗщикъ (jaščik), from ꙗщъ (jašč) + -икъ (-ik), from Old East Slavic ꙗскъ (jaskŭ), from Old Norse askr, from Proto-Germanic *askaz.
